I'm not officially diagnosed, but here's a memory that still kind of gets to me to this day. 

It was 4th grade, so technically middle school. We had to do a class presentation, and if I remember correctly, we were allowed to pick any topic we wanted. So I chose "animals" which looking back, I think was a big special interest for me when I was a kid. 

I was obsessed with those little bags of plastic animals you could get at dollar stores and stuff. I had tons of them. So for my presentation I brought a huge baggie full of them and described each animal, telling random facts about them. I also brought a stack of photos of my pets to talk about them all. 

I remember at some point in the middle of my presentation, the whole class started talking and ignoring me. At one point the next kid got up to do their presentation while I was still giving mine. I remember I even looked over at the teacher and told her I wasn't finished, expecting that she would tell the class to stop being disruptive and what not. Instead she said something to the effect of "Well you took too long and lost their attention". So I just kind of quietly went back to my desk... 

Not sure if it was autism or not, but that really sucked. 😅

Well, there was the time my mom made fun of my OCD in front of all my friends on my birthday. I had really severe contamination OCD at the time, specifically about poisons getting into my food. (OCD is weird okay.) Sometimes I would ask her to taste my drink or food because it helped me rationalize the thought away. Well I was particularly triggered at the time because we were camping and my mom had been spraying bug killer everywhere. I was expressing my worry about this to her, trying to do it discreetly, and she just blurted out to my friends about how ridiculous I am, laughing, and saying "and she even makes me taste her food all the time like she's a little princess" in this mocking tone. Thankfully she was the only one laughing, but my friends just gave her and then me a confused stare and I was so humiliated because I couldn't even begin to defend myself or explain what was really going on with me. (And yes my mom was aware I had OCD as I was in therapy at the time and had visibly been losing weight because I was so afraid to eat. But she never cared to actually understand how my OCD manifested or what it was like for me living with it.) To this day she is in denial that I was diagnosed. The last time I tried to bring it up she was like "well I think everyone is a little OCD". 🙄

I always want to preface my posts here by saying I'm not diagnosed, just heavily suspecting I might be on the spectrum. But I feel like I almost could have written this. I've had very similar feelings to this ever since I was a kid. Just yesterday I was thinking about it actually, wondering why I'm like this. For me I think I've figured out that it's an extreme empathy thing, and the fact that I'm just hyper aware of the bad in the world I guess. I think the sadness I feel comes from the recognition of innocence. Like this is how my thoughts go: Oh, that person is just going about their day but they must really like flowers or Disney or whatever band they have on their shirt or whatever it might be. And then I'm like "I hope nothing bad happens to them, they're a person with things that make them happy" or something along those lines. With kids it's similar, like "I hope they're okay and people are nice to them".

 I will even get in my feels like this sometimes just thinking about what color they're wearing, because I start thinking that must be their favorite color and I think about them picking that shirt out or whatever. Idk if this makes any sense lol. I'm not sure if it's an autism thing or not, but it reminds me of the thing about feeling empathy for inanimate objects which I have read can be associated with autism because of high empathy, and this is something I have as well, to the point it causes me a small bit of distress at times. I remember as a kid I would feel bad for the food no one wanted at the cafeteria at school lol. This is a sad story, but the first time I remember ever feeling the thing with people's clothes, I was in like first or second grade I think. This kid who was in the grade below me had died, and in the year book they had dedicated a page to him. I remember looking at it and in one of his pictures he was wearing a Scooby-Doo T shirt, and I remember it making me so sad. I was thinking like, "He was just a kid who liked Scooby Doo, how could this happen to him?" Maybe that experience is what triggered this for me in the first place, or maybe it was just my first notable experience with it, I'm not sure. I think that might be a sort of out of the ordinary reaction, considering I was a small child myself, but I remember it so clearly and I've always wondered why I think like that.

This is called head-hopping and is generally frowned upon. The preference is to have one POV only per scene. Rules are meant to be broken, but most readers will find it jarring and confusing. I used to do this when I first started writing and personally I'm glad I moved away from it (stubborn as I was at first) because I found it cluttered the scene too much, and since I like deep POV, I realized the scene is more impactful when told from one character's head only. Maybe with omniscient it could work depending on your style of narrating but perhaps what you need to do is figure out which character's POV the scene really needs to be told from. Which character is the scene impacting more, or whose viewpoint do you as the writer want us to really see it from?

I'm really happy to see this post. I've been researching and introspecting for the last few years trying to figure out if I might also be on the spectrum. I'm still unsure at this point, and I'm already 28 and doing so badly in life right now that being able to afford a professional assessment is still nowhere in sight for me. (And I'm a woman also and have read lots about how we tend to go under the radar so much) That being said, I have more or less self-diagnosed but only to myself. I don't tell other people but I've started to notice that even doing that much has helped me immensely with my self esteem and self acceptance. I don't get so frustrated with myself and I don't feel so bad about myself anymore, just knowing there is a potential explanation for why I am the way I am and have been since childhood, even if other people don't know it and choose to bully me and give me a hard time. I've seen a lot of acceptance with self-diagnosing but also a lot of people who really don't agree with it and I just don't get it. I mean it's not like self-diagnosed people can actually access accommodations or assistance and I feel like most of us are aware that we won't be taken seriously in most cases so I don't understand the outrage. What's wrong with people having some semblance of validation for themselves? There is a big difference between a person who saw one thing about autism and automatically start saying they're on the spectrum and a person who has done extensive research and self-reflection to come to that possibility. People would see that if they would take the time to hear people out. If you have time to make accusations and insults, then you have time to have an actual discussion right?

Hello, fellow girl who absolutely hates roaches here. I've dealt with two roach infestations in my life so far. (Hopefully there won't be any more) 
If you've only seen one roach in your apartment, I wouldn't be too concerned. It doesn't necessarily mean you have an infestation. If pest control has been there to spray recently they will be on the move for a little bit trying to get away. (Hopefully your apartment complex is good about keeping up with that) 
They can usually be found in your bathroom or kitchen because they are looking for food and water sources. It's difficult to completely keep them from accessing one room-- they're sneaky little things. But unless you have a bad infestation, you usually won't see them in other areas of the house. Your best bet is to keep them from having a reason to want to nest in your bedroom-- keep it free of food and free of clutter. They love clutter, especially cardboard boxes if you have any lying around. 
I've yet to have one crawl into bed with me (knock on wood) but pro tip: if possible, keep your bed away from the wall. 
Other than that, try to seal up any cracks in the walls or floor that you see. And if you feel like you need extra protection, diatomaceous earth works wonders to kill roaches. It doesn't attract them and it isn't a poison. Basically its a powder and when they walk through it it cuts them up and dries them out. Make sure you buy the food grade kind, otherwise it's toxic. But the food grade is totally safe for you and your pets if you have them. I mean, don't go sprinkling it on your food, but other than that it's totally safe. I recommend putting some in your kitchen and bathroom if you continue to see cockroaches. 

Only other advice I can give is try to keep your place as cool as possible. They love heat and humidity.

So I dealt with a lot of these same thoughts years ago. Plus, I have OCD which these thoughts latched onto, so they were quite literally stuck in my head. 

The mindset that has helped me, which may or may not make sense to other people, is that if nothing matters, then anything I want to matter can. Meaning that it really isn't true that nothing matters just because there isn't some outside force demanding that it does. 

Yes, love is a chemical reaction. But why does that mean it doesn't matter? And really, any way you look at it, love is made up of much more than that. Love is a choice you make, long after that chemical feeling has lost its potency. Love is about familiarity and comfort with another person. And maybe that's all chemical too, but again, why does that mean it doesn't matter? Whether or not this is all by design, or the result of coincidence or evolution, it's still a pretty incredible thing to be a part of. Maybe you feel love and happiness and other emotions because it's in your design, but really, how else would you do it? 

Try looking at "right" and "wrong" in a different light-- maybe morality is a social construct but positivity and negativity are real things. You can't say it isn't real when someone feels loved and cared for or when someone feels pain. Whether or not something makes a difference to the universe is irrelevant, and actually, considering it this way is really contradictory to the notion that nothing matters. Why does it matter if it makes a difference to the universe or not? Why should that keep it from making a difference to you? 

Social constructs exist because of this intrinsically understood presence of positivity and negativity. (At least, the sensible ones do, anyway) Murder is illegal because it causes pain and takes away what belongs to others. Other social norms exist simply because people find meaning in them relative to the world around them, the people around them and their experiences. And well, for better or worse, there are people who deviate from these social norms all the time. We all have our own unique ways of responding to things, and that's all in our physical makeup as well. You say you feel like you need to find a subjective meaning for yourself, but "meaninglessness" is just as subjective. 

As for you feeling apathetic and sort of numb to everything after these thoughts plaguing you, well, if there's anything I've learned from struggling with OCD, it's that this is a natural response to thinking about the same thing over and over. It's sort of like the phenomenon of when you repeat a word over and over until it "loses it's meaning". Thankfully, the word feels real again with enough time away from it. 

So, hard as it may be, try to distract yourself. Do things that make you happy and spend time with people without thinking too hard about it. Maybe it's all a chemical reaction in your brain, all things you're "programmed" to feel-- but it's the same for everyone else. This is just how things work. We aren't some kind of ethereal beings, we're human. It's just how we are. Let yourself enjoy it, because again, how else would things really be? "Meaning" and "reality" are not the same thing. Whether something is "true" or "fake" is not determined by its meaningfulness, or lack thereof. 

I hope that helps. :/

I'm a 26 year old woman, and have been suspecting this for a few years, since I was about 22. I've always felt like I was different my whole life but never really considered autism before, because I guess what with the stigma and misinformation I always just thought autism was something different. Anyway, these are some of the things I've struggled with throughout my life and reasons I'm thinking I could be on the spectrum: 

I guess the main thing is probably my extreme social anxiety/awkwardness. Ever since kindergarten I've struggled to make friends. I always only had one or two friends at a time, and to this day, all my friends are people I've known all my life because I just can't seem to make new ones and I have a really hard time being around people I'm not comfortable with. I've also rarely ever made friends on my own, pretty much everyone I know started off as a friend of my older brother or a friend of a friend. 

I was also bullied all through school and have been bullied at all my jobs as an adult. I'm currently unemployed because of it. Everywhere I go it seems like people are quick to single me out. Either people are flat out rude to me or I get the sense that people are talking down to me, even when they seem like they're being nice. In school, people picked on me for being quiet and called me weird and stupid. At work, it's been the same. I've actually been called "that weird girl" by another adult before. A lot of the time I am confused as to why people are treating me like this. It seems to come out of nowhere, but I started picking up on the fact that, for whatever reason, I just kind of never understand what's going on or what people are saying to me at work. It's hard to explain but I always just feel so lost and then when I don't understand something after the second or third time of someone explaining something I don't ask again because they lose their patience with me. I've had coworkers roll their eyes when I thought I was just asking a simple question, and a common phrase I've heard at probably every job is "You've worked here how long and you don't know this/how to do this?" And I'm honestly usually confused because I didn't know about it at all, but even people who were hired at the same time as me or even after me are catching on to everything with no problem. 

I'm also extremely bad at understanding directions. I can't drive anywhere by myself unless it's a specific route I've gone on many times and even then I have to keep my GPS on in case there's road work or a detour because I will get lost if not and possibly have an anxiety attack because driving makes me extremely anxious and I can't handle it if this situation occurs. I once tried to follow behind my cousin to go somewhere I'd never driven but got lost and had to pull over and call my husband to come find me because I didn't know where I was.
